counterspeech.title: Counterspeech
counterspeech.description: Counterspeech is defined as all communicative actions aimed at refuting hate speech through cogent reasons, and true and fact-bound arguments (Schieb and Preuss, 2016).

dataSources.title: Data sources
dataSources.description: Contains a fact-checking article from a certified publisher (signatory of the IFCN Code of Principles).

dialogue.title: Dialogue
dialogue.description: Create a dialogue that simulates the interaction between someone spreading hate/misinformation and an operator responding with fact-driven arguments.

groundText.title: Ground text spans
groundText.description:
You can add portions of the fact-checking article that support the operator’s reply.

Ground text is automatically added when a turn is generated. You can also manually highlight a part of the article and click the “link” button.

newTurn.title: New turn
newTurn.description:
You can add a new turn in different ways:

  • Add an empty turn with the “+” buttons.
  • Automatically generate a turn using a selected article portion.
  • Select a portion as ground text, then click “Generate from ground”.

Note: Even automatically generated turns and ground text can always be edited.

home.title: Fighting Hate and Disinformation Online
home.description: The Hatedemics platform leverages artificial intelligence to analyze online content, enhance critical thinking, and train responses to hate speech.
home.networkDescription: An interactive map to observe the connections between channels, content, and dynamics related to hate and disinformation online. Discover what happens on the web, follow the flows, and identify the key nodes of toxic communication.
home.counterspeechDescription: Train your ability to respond to hate and disinformation content with targeted writing exercises. Learn how to use reliable sources to create solid arguments and develop your critical thinking to change the tone of online debate.
home.educationalDescription: Explore resources and educational materials to understand and counter online hate.
home.guideDescription: What to know before using the platform.

network.title: Network
network.description: The network shows the connections between the collected telegram channels. A channel is a node and it is connected to another channel if it “recommends” it. Recommendations are generated automatically by Telegram based on the channels' users overlap.

inRec.title: In Recommendations
inRec.description: How much a channel is recommended by other channels.

outRec.title: Out Recommendations
outRec.description: How much a channel recommends other channels.

risk.title: Infodemic Risk
risk.description: How much the channel is reliable. This measure goes from 0 to 1.

check.title: Check Worthiness
check.description: It indicates whether a message can be fact-checked. This means that the message contains facts rather than opinions and is relevant enough to be fact-checked.

telegramDataset.title: Telegram Dataset
telegramDataset.description:
A dataset is a structured collection of data. The platform includes approximately 10 million Telegram messages which were downloaded from around 500 channels, covering 4 languages (English, Italian, Spanish and Polish).

Telegram was chosen as it provides free access to large-scale data collection, unlike other popular messaging platforms.

telegramChannels.title: Telegram Channels and chats
telegramChannels.description:
A Telegram channel is a space where one or a few admins can post messages to a large audience.

A channel can have one or more chats with different settings: for example, some where only admins can publish messages, and others where everyone can participate.

A channel’s chats or conversations refer to the messages posted there and the way audiences react.

network.title: Network
network.description:
A network is a structure that represents entities as points and the relationships between them as lines.

In this network, the downloaded Telegram channels are displayed as points, and lines show how they're connected. A channel is linked to another when Telegram automatically recommends it, based on how many users both channels share.

disinformation.title: Disinformation
disinformation.description: Disinformation is false content shared with the intention of causing harm. The creation of this type of content is most often motivated by the desire to earn money, gain publicity or increase political influence.

reliability.title: Reliability
reliability.description:
Reliability captures how trustworthy and accurate a link is. It is determined through a manual evaluation of the website.

A higher reliability score indicates that the source can be trusted to provide accurate and well-founded information.

infodemicRisk.title: Infodemic Risk
infodemicRisk.description:
The Infodemic Risk tells us how much the channel is reliable, ranging from 0 (completely reliable) to 1 (fully unreliable).

It is based on how reliable the websites shared in the channel are, and how much people in the channel are exposed to those links (it considers the number of views).

A low number means users are exposed to more reliable information!

For more details, you can check out this article.

hateSpeech.title: Hate Speech
hateSpeech.description: Hate Speech is defined as the expression of offensive, discriminatory opinions, content or communications towards specific groups of people or individuals on the basis of their identity characteristics, such as gender, age, sexual orientation, nationality, ethnicity, religion, skin colour, disability or other.

checkWorthyness.title: Check-worthyness
checkWorthyness.description:
Check-Worthy refers to a message, claim, or piece of content that is likely to be of public interest and may require verification by fact-checkers.

A message is considered check-worthy when it:

  • Makes a factual claim that can be verified or disproven,
  • Has the potential to influence opinions, behaviors, or public debate,
  • Addresses sensitive or high-impact topics (e.g. politics, health, security, migration),
  • Or shows signs of possible misinformation or disinformation.

steps.title: What is Hatedemics
steps.html:
Hatedemics is a European project focused on raising awareness about hate speech, disinformation, and how these two issues intersect. The project aims to empower NGOs, civil society organisations, fact-checkers, public authorities, and young people to effectively prevent and combat polarisation, intolerance, and conspiracy theories.

Visit the Hatedemics website to learn more about the project.

steps.title: What does the platform include?
steps.html:
🎓 Educational activities: Test your knowledge on hate speech and misinformation with dedicated interactive exercises!

🌐 Explore Telegram messages: Discover how thousands of Telegram channels connect with an interactive map (Network), see what they’re really talking about (Channel) and how hateful and misleading content from these channels looks like (Conversation).

💬 Counterspeech writing: When and how to reply to misinformation-driven hate speech? Here you can find a dialogue model that simulates the interaction with a hater spreading misinformation, generating fact-based de-escalatory responses called counterspeech.

🌍 Languages: The platform supports 5 languages: English, Spanish, Italian, Maltese and Polish.

steps.title: How does Hatedemics use AI?
steps.html:
• 📊 Data Analysis: It analyzes large volumes of Telegram data to reveal hate speech and disinformation trends. Insights are AI-generated and may be occasionally inaccurate: please consult the referring educators if in doubt.
  • 🤖 Counterspeech dialogue generation: The platform features a dialogue model that simulates interactions with haters, generating “counterspeech” responses to misinformation and hate speech. These AI-generated replies, editable by users, teach when and how to respond with facts.

steps.title: Trigger warning
steps.html: ⚠️ Warning: this platform contains unobfuscated examples some readers may find offensive.

educational.title: Educational Activities
educational.subtitle:
In this section you will find interactive exercises designed to help you understand the mechanisms behind disinformation and hate speech.

You can explore cognitive biases and logical fallacies, practice debunking techniques, learn the principles of the Human Rights Declaration to understand the fundamental rights protecting human dignity, and apply lateral reading skills to critically evaluate online content.

Each activity is an opportunity to train your critical thinking and become more resilient against manipulation and misinformation.
educational.eduCard1Desc: Discover the core principles protecting human dignity.
educational.eduCardBiasDesc: Explore the logical fallacies and cognitive biases behind hate speech and disinformation.
educational.eduCard3Desc: Learn how to debunk  disinformation effectively.
educational.eduCard4Desc: Learn how to read and check online content.
educational.warningText: These activities contain unobfuscated examples some readers may find offensive. If any activity or part of activity makes you feel uncomfortable or you feel triggered please refer to us or feel free to leave the room.

humanRights.title: Human Rights
humanRights.description: The fundamental human rights outlined by the United Nations in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protect and uphold the dignity, equality, and freedom of all people. Some of them are listed below in a simplified version.
humanRights.objectives:
• Developing knowledge about human rights;
  • Rising awareness about connection between human rights and hate speech and disinformation;
  • Learning possible argument for reaction on hate speech and disinformation.
humanRights.task:
Form 12 groups. Each group picks up one card. Each group discusses the meaning of the human right written on their card. After 5 minutes, the first group explains what the right means to them and how it connects to hate speech. The teacher may add to their explanation if needed.
Then, the next group with the following card explains the meaning of their right and its connection to hate speech. Repeat this process until all groups have shared.
humanRights.taskCompleteText: Did you already know all the human rights mentioned? Which ones are new to you? Was it easy or difficult to explain the meaning of these rights and find a link between them and hate speech? Can you name other human rights that were not mentioned?

debunking.title: Debunking
debunking.finalMessage: You have completed the activity! You can now move to the next activity.
debunking.description:
The objective of fact-checking is to provide citizens with tools and information that allow them to form opinions with all the data and verified facts at hand and, consequently, make informed decisions. Misinformation can influence how society thinks and how it deals with everyday problems, and that's why fact-checkers' central mission is to shed light and data on these issues. Broadly speaking, fact-checking involves detecting hoaxes, verifying their content, and spreading the denial.
Fact-checkers work daily on debunking: they verify content and explain why something is false after it’s been shared and viralized in social media. It’s important for the public record and to avoid that more people read, share and believe lies. Some debunkings are very difficult: take lots of time and require the use of specific tools. Others just require a lot of observation and searching for specific reliable information. 
Let´s try! In this exercise you will learn, in a guided way, some debunk techniques and why it's important to activate critical thinking and identify how the viralizing of some hoaxes can create and strengthen disinformation narratives.
debunking.objectives:
Debunk: learn, in a guided way, some debunk techniques.

Develop critical thinking using the pre-bunking strategy: during the exercise, the users discover what are disinformation narratives and can reflect about the most spread ones in their country.

Activate critical thinking: by understanding how the viralizing of some hoaxes can create and strengthen disinformation narratives.
debunking.task: Simulate the actions of a fact-checker by selecting the most effective way to debunk a suspicious content. Can you also identify the related disinformation narrative?

If you look closely at the two photos, it is clear that it is the same photo in two different contexts.

The UK Government facilitates immigration and offers benefits to immigrants

feedback.correct:
Correct!

Disinformation narratives can manipulate us and distort our perception of reality to support an ideology. These are spread through the growing circulation of hoaxes and disinformation content that support them. Not sharing suspicious content and recognizing these narratives helps curb lies and hate speech.

Check out how professional fact-checkers debunked this disinformation:

Maldita.es analysis

When some people think of a fact-checker, they only see a journalist who looks into a claim, checks it and confirms whether it is true or not — the debunking process. Nevertheless, fighting disinformation effectively nowadays takes much more than that: quickly detecting possible hoaxes before they go viral and affect more people; explaining that not everything is black or white, helping people to be well-prepared against falsehoods through Media Literacy or regulation; creating tools to make it harder for others to deceive us, or fighting together against manipulation: this is what we call pre-bunking.

bias.title: Biases and fallacies
bias.description:
Logical fallacies associated with hate speech and disinformation

The content of hate speech and disinformation may sometimes look very convincing. This is because people who perpetuate hate speech often rely on logical fallacies – constructs hate groups use to justify their causes and their belief that people who come across this content would consider it as reasonable and truthful. Logical fallacies can use false premises, true premises but false conclusions, or true premises and conclusions but a false argument. Some fallacies are produced with the intention of deceiving or making misinformation viral.

There are many fallacies that show up in hate speech. Here are some of them:

Argumentum ad populum – a non-substantive way of arguing in which the speaker appeals to the tastes, preferences and prejudices of the crowd. Based on national egoism, instincts, stereotypes or prejudices, the speaker tries to win over the crowd to their thesis (e.g. The majority of people in our country thinks like this, so this is the way we should act);

Ipse dixit – the way of argumenting without providing a valid proof (e.g. the political party said it so it must be true);

A slippery slope fallacy – occurs when someone claims that a position or decision will lead to a series of unintended negative consequences (e.g. we cannot let the migrants stay in our country as they will bring their families here and have children, which will lead us to losing our jobs and the collapse of the social security system, and as a result we will be poor and lose control over our country);

Either-or fallacy – where someone claims there are only two ways of approaching the issue, while there are many other options (e.g. you can either vote for this party or live your life in constant danger);

Post hoc, ergo propter hoc – logical error in wrongly concluding that there is a causal connection between two events merely because one occurred before the other (e.g. Ever since we got a new maths teacher, I’ve been getting bad grades. She must be the reason I’m doing poorly);

Argumentum Ad Hominem – when someone attacks the person making an argument rather than the argument itself (e.g. Don't listen to Peter's opinion on the group project — he's lazy and never does anything right);

Cherry picking – when someone selectively presents evidence that supports their argument while ignoring or dismissing evidence that contradicts it (e.g. \"Hate speech isn't harmful. Look at this one study that says it's just offensive, not dangerous\" - while ignoring dozens of other studies showing the psychological and social harm of hate speech);

Appeal to tradition – when an argument assumes something is good or true simply because it is being traditionally done or believed, without considering whether it is still valid in the present context (e.g. In our school we have always had more men than women in the school council, and it always worked well).

Argument from anecdote – someone uses a single, often personal, experience or story to support a general conclusion or claim (e.g. I don't think hate speech leads to real harm. I’ve heard people make offensive jokes all the time, and no one I know has ever been seriously affected);

Ad ignorantiam fallacy – someone argues that a claim is true or false simply because it has not been proven the opposite (e.g. No one has ever proven that students cheat on online exams, so it must not happen).

Cognitive Biases

Our brain uses shortcuts to help us make quick decisions in everyday life. These shortcuts help us focus only on the most important information, so we don’t get overwhelmed by everything we see and hear. This makes the brain work more efficiently. However, the downside is that these shortcuts can sometimes lead us to make mistakes or misunderstand things because of our thinking (cognitive) biases.

We are all affected by cognitive biases in our decision-making process, and those who spread disinformation understand these biases very well. Here are some examples of cognitive biases:

Membership bias – tendency to favour own group over other groups (e.g. The committee chose to fund the project led by their colleague, even though another proposal was stronger, saying We know and trust our own people.);

Availability bias – tendency to rely on information that comes quickly to mind (e.g. After seeing a news report about plane crashes, someone insists flying is more dangerous than driving, despite statistics showing otherwise);

Causality bias – occurs when people believe that there is a relationship between events that are actually independent of each other (e.g. Every time I wear my lucky socks, my team wins – so they must be the reason).;

Blind spot bias – the tendency to see oneself as less biased than other people (e.g. I’m fair and objective, unlike others who let their feelings get in the way of facts);

Confirmation bias – tendency to search for, interpret, favour and recall information in a way that confirms prior beliefs (e.g. Belief vaccines are dangerous only reads articles that support this view and dismisses scientific research that disproves it.);

Authority bias – tendency to be more influenced by the opinions of authority people (e.g. It must be true – a famous doctor said so on TV – even if there's no supporting evidence.).
bias.objectives:
• Develop awareness about social mechanisms, cognitive biases and logical fallacies
  • Develop critical thinking competence

Social mechanisms, cognitive biases and logical fallacies are factors which help hate speech and disinformation spread. By getting to know some of them, we can be more immune to them and be more critical to other forms of manipulation.

lateralreading.title: Lateral reading
lateralreading.subtitle: Below you can see various screenshots. Think about which one best answers the following question.
lateralreading.description:
Lateral reading is a technique that allows us to quickly assess whether a web page's content comes from reliable sources and is based on quality data, references, and information.

In a research conducted by the Stanford History Education Group, educators discovered that it is an efficient way to assess the quality of an unfamiliar website.

This powerful strategy (used by fact-checkers) to evaluate information online involves not reading a website ‘vertically’, as if it were a printed document, but instead using a method called ‘lateral reading’.

This means analysing the webpage by opening several tabs to answer key questions about the content:
  • Who is the author of the content? Is it an expert source?
  • Can we find evidence? Is it based on facts and data?
  • Is it published by other reliable sources? What do they say about it?

In addition to the above key questions, the lateral reading technique invites us to promote critical thinking and go deeper by analysing other aspects of the content, such as:
  • Who funds or sponsors the site where the original piece was published?
  • What do other authoritative sources say about that site?
  • When you search for the topic of the original piece, are the top results from fact-checking organisations?
  • Have any questions been raised about other articles the author has written?
  • Does the information you find elsewhere contradict the original piece?
  • Are credible news outlets reporting on — or perhaps more importantly, not reporting on — what you are reading?

Lateral reading helps us better evaluate our sources of information — that is, to distinguish between truth and lies — and to consciously exercise our right to choose how we access information.

• Learning about transparency and source credibility factors
  • Developing competence in identifying trustworthy sources of information

feedback.correct: Correct! In Wikipedia we find that ‘The People's Voice (formerly known as ‘NewsPunch’ and ‘Your News Wire’) is an American fake news website based in Los Angeles (screenshot 3). Wikipedia's article shows a list of references, including fact-checkers’ articles and academic investigations that report ‘The People´s Voice’ has published several false stories, including The Pizzagate Conspiracy Theory and Anti-vaccination hoaxes (screenshot 4).

sections.conclusionQuestion: Answer the following questions according to the content presented in the provided screenshots: Was information about the authors provided, and could their expertise be verified? Did the content include evidence supported by facts and data? Was the same information published or confirmed by other reliable sources?
sections.conclusion: After applying the Lateral reading method, we found that ‘The People's Voice’ is not a reliable source. It has the appearance of a media website and publishes content with a ‘Fact Checked stamped’, but in fact, the website publishes misinformation that is shared as real.

inspect.title: Channel overview
inspect.subtitle:
On this page, you can overview the content of a single Telegram channel in detail. The table shows the main topics of the channel, how often they appear in the messages, the percentage of hate speech and check-worthiness within each, and their prevalent sentiment.

On the right, you’ll find key channel information, while the word clouds visualize which terms appear most often in non-hate and hate speech messages, as well as in check-worthy and not check-worthy messages.

Use the filters and buttons to switch views between channels’ chats and topics, or to adjust the type of word cloud you see. If you hover your mouse over any label or button, you’ll see a short explanation of what it does.

channel.title: Telegram Channels Network
channel.subtitle:
Below, you can see a network of Telegram channels where each channel is a point ('node'). These channels are linked when Telegram automatically recommends one to another, usually because they share many of the same users.

You can dive into the network and the table to uncover real-world channels that might be spreading disinformation or hate speech.

Adjust the color and size of the channels, filter and reorder their features to find the ones that interest you most.

If you hover your mouse over any label or button, you’ll see a short description of what it does to help guide you.

conversation.title: Inside the Chats
conversation.subtitle:
On this page, you can explore individual messages from the channel.

Each row in the table shows the message text, its date, and details such as the number of likes, whether it contains hate speech, whether it is considered “check-worthy”, and if one target group is mentioned.

These insights allow you to see not just what kinds of content are being posted, but also how audiences engage with it.
You can filter the messages by hate speech, check-worthiness, or target group to focus on the conversations that interest you most.

You can also reorder the messages by clicking on the column headers.
For example, if you want to see how a conversation developed over time, reorder the table by the Date column.

Hover your mouse over any label or button to see a short explanation of what it does.

networkNavigation.title: Network navigation
networkNavigation.description:
This network displays the collected Telegram channels and their connections.

Use your mouse to drag and zoom across the channel network, and click on a channel to see its details.

When you click, the channel’s connection will light up, an info panel will appear on the right, and an ‘Explore the channel’ button will be activated if its messages can be viewed (i.e. if the channel is expandable).

datasetLanguage.title: Dataset language selection
datasetLanguage.description:
Use the dropdown menu to select the Telegram dataset you intend to explore.

The network will automatically update to show data for your selection, and the chosen language will hold across all three tabs (Network, Channel Overview, and Conversation).

colorSize.title: Color & Size selection
colorSize.description:
Use the color and size options to explore the network. Different settings highlight key features and reveal patterns.

For example, setting color = Infodemic Risk and size = Hate Speech shows high-risk channels in red, with those containing more hate speech appearing larger.

nodeStats.title: Node Statistics
nodeStats.description:
This table shows the data for every channel in the network. You have two main interactions:
  • Sort the Table: Click on any column title (e.g., Number of messages) to reorder the data.
  • Find a Channel: Click on any row to highlight that channel on the network map and open its info panel.

explored.title: Expandable
explored.description:
A channel is expanded if we collect all its chat messages, shown in the Conversation page.

Not expandable channels are shown in blue in the network.

exploreChannel.title: ‘Explore channel’ button
exploreChannel.description: Click the ‘Explore channel’ button to move to the chat topics page and see further information and a detailed breakdown of the topics discussed in that channel's chats.

degreeCentrality.title: Degree centrality
degreeCentrality.description:
Shows how many direct connections a point (which for us is a Telegram channel) has in the network.

This helps to figure out how “important” it is — think popularity: lots of friends!

communities.title: Communities
communities.description:
In network science, communities are natural groups within the networks.

To detect them, we use the Louvain community detection method, which looks for groups where there are many connections inside the group.
(Like a friend group where everyone knows each other very well!)

For more details, you can check out this article.

topic.title: Topic
topic.description: Starting from all the messages in the selected chat, the most significant topics are extracted using AI-based topic modeling: messages are grouped together based on similarities in their content. These clusters reveal the most relevant themes of discussion, helping to identify what people are talking about in the channel.

hateSpeechPercent.title: Hate Speech %
hateSpeechPercent.description: Using AI-based classification, each message in a channel is analyzed to detect whether it contains hate speech (see the Glossary for more information about the definition of Hate Speech). By calculating the average Hate Speech within the messages related to each topic, we can highlight the prevalence of hate speech within the conversations.

checkWorthinessPercent.title: Check-Worthiness %
checkWorthinessPercent.description: Using AI-based classification, each message in a channel is analyzed to detect whether it is check-worthy, meaning it contains claims or statements that may require fact-checking (see the Glossary for more on Check-Worthiness). By calculating the average level of check-worthy content within each topic, we highlight the prevalence of potentially misleading or questionable claims in the conversations.

prevalentSentiment.title: Prevalent sentiment
prevalentSentiment.description: Using AI-based sentiment analysis, each message in a channel is classified as neutral, positive, or negative. By aggregating the sentiment of all messages related to a topic, we identify the prevalent sentiment of that topic.

wordCloud.title: Word Cloud
wordCloud.description:
A word cloud is a visual representation of the most frequent words in a collection of text: the more often a word appears, the larger it is displayed in the cloud.

Use it to visualize which terms appear most often in non-hate and hate speech messages, and in check-worthy and not check-worthy messages, at chat or topic level.

reactions.title: Reactions
reactions.description: The total number of reactions (like, dislikes, heart and so on) a message received. It’s an indication of the popularity of a message.

reliability.title: Reliability
reliability.description: Indicates the average reliability of the urls contained in the message. It is automatically assessed according to the url domain: can be reliable, unreliable, or unknown.

target.title: Target
target.description:
A target refers to the individual or group of people mentioned in a message. In this project, we identify whether a message contains a reference to one of the following groups: black people, LGBTQIA+, Jews, migrants, Muslims, people with disabilities, women.

The presence of a target does not by itself imply hate, but it allows further filtering to see which messages mentioning these groups are also hateful, checkworthy, or contain unreliable links.

filtersTable.title: Filters and Table Headers
filtersTable.description:
Use the three filters (Hate Speech, Check Worthy, and Filter by Target) to display only the related rows.
You can also click on the table headers to sort the rows by the presence or absence of a specific variable.

startConversation.title: Start conversation
startConversation.details: Press this button to choose a topic for counterspeech writing. You’ll then be redirected to the counterspeech writing page.
